evaluated.name: Double Confirmation Value Payout
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Mispricing is revealed only when the price-based and management-based valuation signals agree: firms that are simultaneously in the cheap tail and the net-repurchase tail are genuinely undervalued, firms simultaneously in the expensive tail and the net-issuance tail are genuinely overvalued, and firms where the two disagree (cheap issuers, expensive repurchasers) carry no reliable information and should be pushed to the middle of the distribution.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the additive SUMRANK with a conjunctive MIN of ranks makes the score a true AND-operator: the "both good" term only rises when the weaker of the two dimensions rises, and subtracting the symmetric "both bad" conjunction builds the short leg from expensive issuers rather than from any firm with a low sum. Because disagreement cases collapse to a neutral score, the long-short spread is by construction an interaction portfolio and cannot be replicated by any weighted average of book-to-market and payout yield.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Book Equity Retired Per Market Dollar
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MUL(SUB(prstkc, sstk), ceq), MUL(MUL(prcc_f, csho), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The per-share value created by a buyback equals the dollars spent times the discount at which shares are retired, so a dollar of repurchase transfers far more book value to remaining holders when price-to-book is low; symmetrically, a firm that sells equity below book destroys per-share value and is signalling financing desperation rather than opportunistic timing.
evaluated.reasoning: This is an inherently multiplicative quantity — net repurchase yield scaled by the inverse of the market-to-book multiple — so it cannot be decomposed into the value and payout anomalies acting separately, and it replaces the earlier noisy binary SIGN moderator with a continuous, economically interpretable intensity. The long tail is cheap aggressive repurchasers and the short tail is cheap aggressive issuers, which is the value-destruction case the accretion arithmetic actually identifies, not the sign-flip artifact the critic correctly rejected.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Self Funded Payout At Cheap Enterprise Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is not payout itself but its funding source: cheap enterprises returning capital out of internally generated cash while also retiring debt are shrinking total claims from strength, whereas cheap enterprises whose payout is financed by new borrowing, or which must raise net external capital, are levering into a discount and are value traps.
evaluated.reasoning: The valuation leg now enters as a non-negative rank multiplier on the signed capital-return flow, so the signal is a genuine conditional statement — capital-return intensity is priced only where the enterprise is cheap on EBITDA/EV — rather than the additive rank blend the critic flagged. Both numerator and denominator of the financing leg are now measured at enterprise value, fixing the inconsistent equity-market-cap scaling, and subtracting net debt issuance strips out debt-funded buybacks that mimic the signal without any real contraction of claims.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Contrarian Buyback At Own Valuation Low
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Managerial conviction is most informative when it is contrarian relative to the firm's own valuation history: buying back stock when the firm trades at the cheap end of its own five-year book-to-market range reveals private information that the decline is unwarranted, whereas issuing equity precisely at the firm's own valuation trough reveals a binding financing constraint.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the horizon-smoothing tweak the critic rejected and replaces the cross-sectional value dimension with a within-firm, time-series valuation position, so the signal identifies a timing decision rather than re-sorting on the level of book-to-market or composite issuance. Because TS_RANK is firm-relative it is orthogonal to the size and style tilts that drive standard value-plus-buyback composites, and the multiplicative form means firms at their own valuation highs receive near-zero scores regardless of payout.

evaluated.name: Rich Valuation Equity Issuance Intensity
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), WINSOR(RATIO(sstk, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts poor returns mainly because managers time it to windows of overvaluation, so the same dollar of stock sold is far more bearish when the firm trades at a high market-to-book multiple; issuance by low-multiple firms is closer to genuine financing need and carries much weaker negative information.
evaluated.reasoning: The direction is now internally consistent: the non-negative expensiveness rank amplifies issuance intensity, so richly valued heavy issuers earn the highest scores and the EXPECTED_SIGN is negative, placing them in the short leg exactly as the market-timing story requires. Replacing raw csho growth with cash-flow-statement equity sales scaled by market capitalization eliminates the split and stock-dividend contamination the critic identified while keeping a continuous, well-populated distribution.

evaluated.name: Cash Yield Conditional Deleveraging
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high operating cash-flow yield is a discount only if the firm is not consuming that cash to service an expanding debt load; cheap, cash-generative firms that are repaying long-term debt are deleveraging toward a re-rating, while cheap, cash-generative firms simultaneously raising net new debt are distress-financed and their apparent yield reflects credit risk rather than mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: The structure is now multiplicative rather than an additive pairing of cash-flow-to-price with Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan external financing, and the financing leg is restricted to the long-term debt channel so it does not duplicate the equity-issuance signals elsewhere in the batch. Conditioning concentrates the bet inside the high-cash-yield group, where the value-trap versus true-discount distinction is economically live, while expensive firms receive scores near zero and stay out of both legs.

evaluated.name: Buyback Surprise Among Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 1), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: The information content of a buyback is in the change, not the level: mature firms repurchase every year and that steady-state flow is already in prices and in the investment factor, whereas a cheap firm that sharply steps up net repurchase activity relative to last year is delivering new evidence that management sees the discount as unwarranted.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the payout level with a first difference strips the persistent component that loads on CMA and leaves a news-like variable, which is the most direct repair of the alpha-absorption failure diagnosed above. Scaling the flow by assets rather than market value keeps the change from being mechanically driven by the price move already embedded in the valuation moderator, so the two legs of the interaction stay economically independent.

evaluated.name: Industry Relative Cheap Self Funded Payout
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Enterprise multiples are set at the industry level, so a firm cheap relative to its own industry peers while returning capital funded internally rather than by new borrowing is mispriced, whereas the raw cross-sectional EV multiple mostly ranks industries and therefore reproduces a static value tilt.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates one specific design choice against the best generation-0 result (fmb 3.90, alpha +0.010): swapping the cross-sectional rank for an industry rank in the valuation moderator, holding the internally-funded capital-return leg fixed. If the industry-neutral version raises the FF5 alpha while keeping the slope, it confirms that the missing alpha was an industry/value-tilt artifact rather than a defect of the payout-funding mechanism.

evaluated.name: Cheap Firm Buyback Over Dividend Tilt
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Payout composition, not payout size, encodes valuation opinion: dividends are a smoothed commitment insensitive to price, while repurchases are discretionary and price-contingent, so a cheap firm tilting its payout mix toward buybacks and away from dividends is expressing a view that its own shares are the best available investment.
evaluated.reasoning: Total payout yield is a known, factor-spanned characteristic, but the buyback-versus-dividend mix is roughly payout-neutral and therefore should not inherit the HML/CMA loadings that flattened the generation-0 alphas. Conditioning the mix on cheapness gives the interaction its economic bite, since a buyback tilt at a rich valuation carries the opposite information about managerial judgment.

evaluated.name: Net Cash Valuation Repurchase
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a large fraction of market capitalization is covered by net cash on the balance sheet, the operating business is being valued at almost nothing; management repurchasing shares in that state is converting excess liquidity into the cheapest asset it can buy, while a firm in the same state issuing equity signals that the cash is committed or the business is impaired.
evaluated.reasoning: Net cash to price is a valuation metric that HML (book-to-market) spans poorly because book equity mixes cash with operating assets, so the value tilt that absorbed prior alphas should be much weaker here. The interaction is economically necessary: high net cash alone is a known low-return "cash trap" characteristic, and it only becomes bullish when management demonstrably deploys the cash into its own undervalued equity.

evaluated.name: Cheap Equity For Debt Swap
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(MIN(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: When managers believe their equity is cheap relative to their debt, the value-maximizing action is a capital-structure swap — raise long-term debt and retire shares — so a cheap firm doing both simultaneously is making a costly, leverage-increasing bet on its own stock, while a cheap firm doing the reverse swap (selling equity to repay debt) is deleveraging under duress and confirms the discount is warranted.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing leg is no longer a net payout yield, so this is not a rescaling of book-equity-retired-per-market-dollar: the MIN operator requires both debt issuance and equity retirement to be positive, isolating genuine recapitalizations from ordinary cash-funded buybacks and from debt raised to fund capex. Direction is now internally coherent — the non-negative cheapness rank means overvalued issuers sit near zero rather than in the long leg — and the signal deliberately contrasts with the accepted self-funded-payout proposal, so the batch tells us whether the funding source of a buyback helps or hurts.

evaluated.name: Unlevered Cheap Repurchaser
evaluated.expression: MUL(MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness means mispricing only when the firm has the balance-sheet slack to act on it: a low-leverage firm trading at a high book-to-market that retires equity is buying a discount it can afford, whereas an equally cheap but heavily indebted firm is priced for leverage risk and its financing choices are dictated by creditors rather than by managerial valuation opinion.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops all past-return and valuation-change conditioning, so it is not a horizon variant of the contrarian-buyback signal; the new conditioning axis is the leverage state, a financing-theme variable that separates distressed value from mispriced value. Because the MIN conjunction damps highly levered deep-value names — exactly the firms whose returns FF5's HML and CMA loadings already explain — the surviving spread should be less factor-spanned and more likely to show abnormal return rather than a repackaged value tilt.

evaluated.name: Industry Neutral Both Legs Capital Return
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Payout and issuance norms are as industry-specific as valuation multiples — utilities and banks systematically pay out, biotech and tech systematically issue — so the informative part of a firm's capital-return decision is its deviation from peer practice, and pairing that deviation with industry-relative cheapness should isolate firm-specific managerial conviction.
evaluated.reasoning: Industry-ranking only the valuation leg already lifted alpha from 0.010 to 0.014 and Sharpe from 0.35 to 0.42, so the natural next question is whether the residual factor exposure sits in the financing leg's industry composition. IND_ADJ demeans the capital-return intensity within industry while preserving its sign and magnitude, which keeps the economic content intact and removes the sector bets that likely load on CMA and RMW.

evaluated.name: Cash Conversion Enterprise Yield Capital Return
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: EBITDA overstates distributable cash for firms with heavy working-capital absorption or non-cash revenue, so measuring enterprise cheapness with realized operating cash flow should identify firms whose capital return is genuinely fundable and screen out accrual-inflated cheap multiples.
evaluated.reasoning: The financing leg is held fixed against the archive's best signal so the comparison isolates the quality of the valuation numerator, which matters because the mechanism claims the payout is internally funded — a claim EBITDA cannot verify but oancf can. If cash-flow yield strengthens both the slope and the alpha, it tells us the interaction is really about funded conviction rather than about the accounting multiple.

evaluated.name: Dividend Commitment Increase At Cheap Enterprise Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(dvt, 1), at), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Dividends are a sticky commitment that management is reluctant to reverse, so raising the dividend is a costlier and more credible statement about future cash flow than a discretionary buyback; a cheap enterprise increasing its dividend is signalling durable earnings power, while a cheap enterprise cutting it is confirming impairment.
evaluated.reasoning: No archive signal uses the dividend-change channel — all financing legs so far are repurchase, issuance, or debt flows — so this tests a distinct information mechanism (commitment signaling versus opportunistic timing) inside the valuation frame that has worked best. Using the asset-scaled first difference rather than dividend growth keeps non-payers in the sample at zero, preserving coverage while letting initiations and cuts drive the tails.

evaluated.name: Sustained Claim Contraction At Cheap Enterprise Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), 3), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of self-funded capital return can be a one-off recapitalization or an asset-sale artifact, whereas three consecutive years of shrinking total claims while trading cheap identifies a management team with a standing policy of buying its own undervalued capital, which should be both more persistent and more slowly priced by the market.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a horizon ablation of the winning family, justified by evidence rather than by novelty: the one-year version's alpha (0.014, t 1.42) is economically meaningful but imprecise, and if the imprecision comes from year-to-year lumpiness in repurchase and debt flows, cumulating three years of the same construct should raise ls_talpha and Sharpe without changing the economic story. If instead the alpha falls, we learn the signal is news-driven, which would redirect the search toward the change-based designs.

evaluated.name: Financing Direction Purity At Cheap Book Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), ADD(ADD(prstkc, sstk), dvt)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: The credibility of a financing signal lies in its direction relative to total capital-market activity, not its dollar size: a cheap firm whose entire gross activity is share retirement, with no offsetting issuance, is making an unambiguous valuation statement, whereas a cheap firm churning stock in both directions is running option programs rather than expressing conviction.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the payout-composition signal that produced alpha 0.021 with a null slope: normalizing by gross activity (prstkc + sstk + dvt) makes the measure bounded and scale-free, so it is no longer dominated by repurchase intensity and no longer inherits the size and investment-factor loadings that flatten yield-based versions. Because the moderator is a bounded direction score rather than a yield, the resulting spread should be much less collinear with CMA, giving the interaction a cleaner chance at FF5 alpha and a nonzero cross-sectional slope.

evaluated.name: Own Equity Versus Real Investment Choice
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), GROWTH(at, 1)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Every financing decision is a revealed-preference statement about the firm's opportunity set: when a cheaply valued enterprise chooses to retire its own shares while holding or shrinking its asset base, management is stating that its own equity is a better investment than any project it could fund, whereas a cheaply valued firm simultaneously expanding assets and selling stock is stating the opposite and is usually diluting shareholders into low-return growth.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new hypothesis rather than a one-term deletion — the financing leg is now a *contrast* between two competing uses of capital (share retirement versus asset expansion) instead of a payout yield, so it cannot collapse to the published shareholder-yield anomaly crossed with value. The interaction is economically necessary because the same allocation choice carries opposite information at rich valuations, and because the differenced construction nets out the common scale of the firm's financing activity, it should carry less mechanical CMA loading than either component alone.

evaluated.name: Within Cheap Capital Return Conditional
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), 0.7), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms the market already prices as cheap on enterprise cash earnings, the financing decision is the variable that separates genuine mispricing from justified discount: cheap firms retiring claims out of internal cash are undervalued, cheap firms raising net external capital are impaired, and this comparison should hold with no help from the value premium itself.
evaluated.reasoning: The hard indicator switches the financing signal on only inside the cheapest 30% of the cross-section, so both the long and short legs are drawn from the same valuation stratum and the HML/CMA loadings that absorbed 3 percentage points of raw return in the archive's best signal should largely cancel. This is a structural fix for the diagnosed absorption problem rather than a new characteristic, and it makes the surviving spread interpretable as the pure within-value financing effect.

evaluated.name: Within Expensive Net Issuance Conditional
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.7), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Overvaluation is only actionable when management acts on it: within the richly valued 30% of the market, the firms selling stock are cashing in on the premium and should underperform the otherwise identical rich firms that are buying stock back, so the issuance effect exists conditional on high valuation and not merely as a proxy for being a growth stock.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's rich-valuation issuance signal produced a wrong-signed FF5 alpha (+0.048) precisely because its long and short legs straddled the valuation spectrum, handing FF5 enormous negative HML/RMW loadings to price; restricting both legs to expensive firms removes that gradient. This is the short-side counterpart to Signal 1 and, evaluated alongside it, tells us whether the interaction's abnormal return lives in the undervalued corner, the overvalued corner, or both.

evaluated.name: Drawdown Repurchase Conviction
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(prcc_f, TS_MAX(prcc_f, 5)))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Managers know their own reservation price better than any accounting ratio conveys: buying back stock when the price sits far below its own five-year peak is a direct statement that the drawdown is unwarranted, whereas selling equity into the same drawdown signals that the decline reflects real deterioration and a binding need for cash.
evaluated.reasoning: The conditioning variable is a pure price-history state with no accounting input, so unlike book-to-market it is not spanned by HML — and FF5 contains no momentum or drawdown factor at all, which is where the alpha in this family has repeatedly leaked away. It differs from the archive's contrarian-buyback signal because that used the time-series rank of book-to-market, which is contaminated by book-equity growth and is a much noisier proxy for distance from peak valuation.

evaluated.name: Non Liquidating Cheap Capital Return
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(GROWTH(at, 1)), 0.3), MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The capital-return signal means something different in a shrinking business than in a stable one: among firms that are not liquidating their asset base, returning capital out of internal cash is a statement of surplus earnings power, whereas the same statistic in a contracting firm is simply asset runoff that the investment factor already prices.
evaluated.reasoning: Growth now enters as a sample restriction rather than a multiplicative amplifier, so both legs are drawn from the same non-shrinking population — the short leg is a non-liquidating cheap firm raising external capital, not a fast-growing issuer, which removes the asset-growth-anomaly restatement the critic identified. Excluding only the bottom 30% of asset growth keeps roughly seventy percent of firms eligible, so portfolio composition stays broad and stable rather than concentrating in a rare triple-condition corner.

evaluated.name: Stability Weighted Cheap Capital Return
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltis, sstk), ADD(dltr, prstkc)), at), 5))), MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A financing decision is credible evidence about valuation only when it reflects deliberate policy rather than external circumstance, so the current capital-return choice of a cheap firm should be weighted by how stable that firm's external financing has been: steady self-funders are making a judgment, while firms whose capital-market activity lurches year to year are being pushed around by lenders and markets.
evaluated.reasoning: The sign inconsistency is fixed — stability now enters as a nonnegative rank weight multiplying the *signed* capital-return flow, so the long leg is cheap, stable, capital-returning firms and the short leg is cheap, stable, capital-raising firms, with erratic financiers damped toward zero instead of dominating either tail. Measuring volatility on an asset-scaled flow ratio rather than on dollar amounts removes the mechanical size confound, and the weight is a cross-sectional rank so general firm-level volatility enters only through its ordering, not its level.

evaluated.name: Cash Hoard Deployed Into Cheap Equity
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), RATIO(DELTA(che, 1), at)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a cheaply valued firm draws down its cash balance to retire its own shares, it is converting a zero-return asset into a claim it believes is discounted — the strongest available form of managerial conviction; the opposite behavior, accumulating cash while issuing equity at a discount, signals either agency problems or an anticipated need for liquidity.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a rescaling of the incumbent: the financing leg combines a cash-flow-statement buyback with a balance-sheet cash *change*, so it distinguishes payout financed by deploying an existing hoard from routine payout out of current earnings, a distinction none of the archive signals can make. evaluated.expression: ADD(MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), ADD(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1), ABS(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1)))), MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)))), SUB(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1), ABS(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1)))))

evaluated.name: Cheap Given Profitability Capital Return
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, at)))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: A low multiple is only evidence of mispricing when the underlying business is not correspondingly weak, so the informative valuation state is cheapness *relative to operating profitability* — and a firm that is cheap conditional on its profitability while returning capital out of internal cash is the cleanest case of managerial information contradicting the market.
evaluated.reasoning: The moderator is a difference between an HML-aligned rank and an RMW-aligned rank, so by construction it is close to orthogonal to both factors that have been absorbing this family's spread — a direct attack on the alpha leakage rather than another rescaling of the financing leg. The outer RANK keeps the weight nonnegative so the sign structure of the interaction remains the intended one, with cheap-given-profitability repurchasers long and cheap-given-profitability capital raisers short.

evaluated.name: Cash Backed Earnings Behind The Buyback
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at))), MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Management's financing signal is only as credible as the earnings behind it: when a cheap firm returns capital while its reported income is fully backed by operating cash, the buyback is funded by real cash generation, whereas the same buyback at a firm whose income is mostly accruals is more likely earnings-per-share management than a valuation statement.
evaluated.reasoning: This adds a credibility dimension no archive signal contains — the accrual gap between ib and oancf — as a nonnegative weight on the working interaction, so the sign structure is preserved while low-quality-earnings repurchasers are damped toward the middle. It is a genuinely different economic mechanism (verification of the signal's funding) rather than another valuation or scaling variant, and accrual quality is not a Fama-French factor, so any incremental spread should survive the five-factor adjustment.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Flow Capped Buyback At Cheap Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(MIN(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), RATIO(oancf, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: A repurchase is only a credible valuation statement to the extent it is covered by the cash the business actually produces, so the effective signal is the smaller of the net repurchase yield and the operating cash yield: firms buying back beyond their cash generation get no extra credit, and firms with weak or negative cash flow are pushed into the short leg regardless of how much stock they retire.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN operator implements funding capacity as a binding cap rather than as the incumbent's linear subtraction of net debt issuance, so the mechanism is tested in a structurally different way and cash-flow-negative repurchasers — the most likely source of false positives in the archive's long leg — are reclassified rather than merely penalized. Both arguments are EV-scaled, consistent with the empirical regularity that asset-scaled financing legs have systematically delivered negative FF5 alphas in this archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Which Claim Gets Retired At Cheap Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(prstkc, sstk), SUB(dltr, dltis)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm with cash to deploy must choose which claim on the enterprise to buy back, and that choice is a relative-value judgment: a cheap firm retiring equity rather than debt is saying its own stock is the more discounted claim, while a cheap firm that pays down debt instead is saying the opposite — either because it sees no equity discount or because creditors, not managers, are directing the cash.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the economic opposite of the incumbent's financing leg, not a rescaling of it: the incumbent *adds* debt retirement to equity retirement as evidence of claim contraction, whereas this signal *subtracts* it, so the two cannot be near-collinear and evaluating them jointly identifies whether the mechanism is total-claim shrinkage or an equity-versus-debt relative-value choice. Keeping enterprise-value scaling respects the archive regularity that asset-scaled financing legs have delivered significantly negative FF5 alphas while EV-scaled legs have delivered positive ones.

evaluated.name: All Cash Credibility Capital Return

evaluated.hypothesis: If the credibility mechanism is real, then the enterprise should be judged cheap on the same cash that funds the capital return: a firm trading at a low multiple of realized operating cash flow, whose accounting income is fully cash-backed, and which is retiring claims out of that cash, is the internally consistent version of managerial conviction, whereas the EBITDA multiple can be cheap for firms whose earnings never convert to cash.
evaluated.reasoning: The accrual weight and the cash-flow multiple restrict the sample identically (both need oancf), so this costs no additional coverage relative to the 0.078 winner while making the valuation leg consistent with the credibility story. It directly tests whether the gain from generation 4 comes from cash-based measurement generally or specifically from the accrual gap.

evaluated.hypothesis: Management can only credibly commit cash to retiring claims when its earnings stream is predictable; a cheap firm with stable profitability that returns capital is acting on information about a durable business, while the same action at a firm with wildly variable earnings is as likely to be a lucky-year windfall as a valuation judgment.

evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm that returns capital while carrying little near-term maturing debt is spending genuinely discretionary cash, whereas the same action by a firm whose capital structure is dominated by short-dated obligations is fragile — the payout may be reversed at the next refinancing, and the discount may reflect rollover risk the market prices correctly.

evaluated.reasoning: The sign inconsistency is repaired by giving each side its own quality weight — the positive-payout part is scaled by cheapness times *low* accruals, and the negative part by richness times *high* accruals — so low-credibility issuers are pushed further into the short leg instead of being shrunk toward zero. If the alpha survives at full coverage the credibility channel is confirmed as general; if it collapses, the mechanism is specific to cash-flow-statement measurement and we should stop trying to extend it.

evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings credibility validates the payout decision specifically, because dividends and repurchases are the discretionary acts management chooses on the basis of its own valuation view, whereas net debt issuance is largely determined by lenders and refinancing schedules and therefore cannot be certified by the quality of reported income.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a blind ablation but a directed test of the mechanism's boundary: the credibility story is about managerial discretion, so if the accrual weight interacts with the shareholder-payout component and merely adds noise through the debt component, dropping the debt term should raise both the slope and the alpha. evaluated.hypothesis: A revenue-based enterprise multiple identifies firms whose operating scale is cheaply priced without conditioning on current margins, so it captures temporarily depressed but structurally sound businesses that an EBITDA multiple classifies as expensive; combined with credible earnings and capital return, this should locate mispricing that profitability-linked value measures miss.

evaluated.hypothesis: Credibility belongs inside the financing measure, not beside it: the economically meaningful quantity is the capital a cheap firm returns in excess of the paper earnings it booked without collecting, so subtracting the accrual gap from the capital-return flow yields a single measure of claim contraction that is actually financed by realized cash.

evaluated.hypothesis: The economically relevant quantity may be how far this year's capital return departs from the firm's own normal level, in real magnitude rather than in rank order — a firm that ordinarily returns one percent of assets and this year returns eight is making a much larger statement than one that moves from the fortieth to the eightieth percentile of a narrow personal range.

evaluated.hypothesis: The overvaluation half of the story should obey the same within-firm logic: a richly valued firm raising equity and debt at the top of its own five-year fundraising range is exploiting a window it does not normally have, whereas a firm whose capital raising is at its habitual level is simply running its standard financing policy and carries no timing information.

evaluated.reasoning: Position within a range and slope through it are distinct temporal concepts: a firm can sit at its five-year high after one lumpy year with no trend, or trend strongly upward without hitting an extreme, so this is not a horizon variant of the generation-6 winner but a different statement about the financing process. evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)))

evaluated.name: Compressing Multiple With Rising Payout
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(TREND(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 5)), WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1))

evaluated.name: Rising Payout Long Rising Raising Short
evaluated.expression: ADD(MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), ADD(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1), ABS(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1)))), MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)))), NEG(ADD(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 5), 1), ABS(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 5), 1))))))

evaluated.name: Two Sided Trajectory Against Multiple Path
evaluated.expression: ADD(MUL(RANK(TREND(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 5)), ADD(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1), ABS(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1)))), MUL(RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 5))), SUB(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1), ABS(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1)))))

evaluated.name: Debt Repayment Trajectory At Cheap Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(dltr, dltis), at), 5), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: For a cheaply valued and leveraged business, the multi-year path of debt repayment is the financing decision that matters most: steadily rising net repayment transfers enterprise value from creditors to shareholders and removes the risk that justified the discount, whereas a steadily rising reliance on new borrowing is the path toward the distress the market fears.
evaluated.reasoning: Every trajectory result so far has used a flow dominated by shareholder payout, so this isolates whether the mechanism is shareholder orientation specifically or a general policy of claim retirement — a question the level-based tests could not answer because levels of debt flows were absorbed by the investment factor. evaluated.name: Accelerating Capital Return When Cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(ACCEL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at)), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: If the market underreacts to gradual shifts in shareholder orientation, it should underreact most where the shift is speeding up: a cheap firm whose capital return is not merely rising but rising at an increasing rate is in the early, least-recognised phase of a policy change, and the second derivative should lead the first.
evaluated.reasoning: Position, level-deviation and slope have all now been tested, and acceleration is the one remaining temporal object in this family — it is distinct because a firm can have a strong five-year slope that is flattening (late, already priced) or a modest slope that is steepening (early, unpriced). evaluated.name: Payout Mix Shift Toward Buybacks When Cheap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at), 5), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Dividends are a price-insensitive commitment while repurchases are a price-contingent investment in the firm's own shares, so a cheap company that has spent five years steadily shifting its payout mix away from dividends and toward buybacks is revealing a strengthening view that its stock is the best available use of cash — whereas a cheap firm drifting the other way is signalling that management sees no such opportunity.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a rescaling of an existing signal: the financing object is the *composition* of payout rather than its total, and the archive's one composition test was measured in levels, where it produced a suggestive alpha (0.021, t 1.58) alongside a completely flat cross-sectional slope (0.20). considered.name: Double Confirmation Value Payout
considered.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))))
considered.hypothesis: Mispricing is revealed only when the price-based and management-based valuation signals agree: firms that are simultaneously in the cheap tail and the net-repurchase tail are genuinely undervalued, firms simultaneously in the expensive tail and the net-issuance tail are genuinely overvalued, and firms where the two disagree (cheap issuers, expensive repurchasers) carry no reliable information and should be pushed to the middle of the distribution.

Because disagreement cases collapse to a neutral score, the long-short spread is by construction an interaction portfolio and cannot be replicated by any weighted average of book-to-market and payout yield.

considered.name: Book Equity Retired Per Market Dollar
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MUL(SUB(prstkc, sstk), ceq), MUL(MUL(prcc_f, csho), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The per-share value created by a buyback equals the dollars spent times the discount at which shares are retired, so a dollar of repurchase transfers far more book value to remaining holders when price-to-book is low; symmetrically, a firm that sells equity below book destroys per-share value and is signalling financing desperation rather than opportunistic timing.
considered.reasoning: This is an inherently multiplicative quantity — net repurchase yield scaled by the inverse of the market-to-book multiple — so it cannot be decomposed into the value and payout anomalies acting separately, and it replaces the earlier noisy binary SIGN moderator with a continuous, economically interpretable intensity. The long tail is cheap aggressive repurchasers and the short tail is cheap aggressive issuers, which is the value-destruction case the accretion arithmetic actually identifies, not the sign-flip artifact the critic correctly rejected.

considered.name: Self Funded Payout At Cheap Enterprise Value
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is not payout itself but its funding source: cheap enterprises returning capital out of internally generated cash while also retiring debt are shrinking total claims from strength, whereas cheap enterprises whose payout is financed by new borrowing, or which must raise net external capital, are levering into a discount and are value traps.
considered.reasoning: The valuation leg now enters as a non-negative rank multiplier on the signed capital-return flow, so the signal is a genuine conditional statement — capital-return intensity is priced only where the enterprise is cheap on EBITDA/EV — rather than the additive rank blend the critic flagged. Both numerator and denominator of the financing leg are now measured at enterprise value, fixing the inconsistent equity-market-cap scaling, and subtracting net debt issuance strips out debt-funded buybacks that mimic the signal without any real contraction of claims.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Contrarian Buyback At Own Valuation Low
considered.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Managerial conviction is most informative when it is contrarian relative to the firm's own valuation history: buying back stock when the firm trades at the cheap end of its own five-year book-to-market range reveals private information that the decline is unwarranted, whereas issuing equity precisely at the firm's own valuation trough reveals a binding financing constraint.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the horizon-smoothing tweak the critic rejected and replaces the cross-sectional value dimension with a within-firm, time-series valuation position, so the signal identifies a timing decision rather than re-sorting on the level of book-to-market or composite issuance. Because TS_RANK is firm-relative it is orthogonal to the size and style tilts that drive standard value-plus-buyback composites, and the multiplicative form means firms at their own valuation highs receive near-zero scores regardless of payout.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Rich Valuation Equity Issuance Intensity
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), WINSOR(RATIO(sstk, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts poor returns mainly because managers time it to windows of overvaluation, so the same dollar of stock sold is far more bearish when the firm trades at a high market-to-book multiple; issuance by low-multiple firms is closer to genuine financing need and carries much weaker negative information.
considered.reasoning: The direction is now internally consistent: the non-negative expensiveness rank amplifies issuance intensity, so richly valued heavy issuers earn the highest scores and the EXPECTED_SIGN is negative, placing them in the short leg exactly as the market-timing story requires. Replacing raw csho growth with cash-flow-statement equity sales scaled by market capitalization eliminates the split and stock-dividend contamination the critic identified while keeping a continuous, well-populated distribution.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash Yield Conditional Deleveraging
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A high operating cash-flow yield is a discount only if the firm is not consuming that cash to service an expanding debt load; cheap, cash-generative firms that are repaying long-term debt are deleveraging toward a re-rating, while cheap, cash-generative firms simultaneously raising net new debt are distress-financed and their apparent yield reflects credit risk rather than mispricing.
considered.reasoning: The structure is now multiplicative rather than an additive pairing of cash-flow-to-price with Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan external financing, and the financing leg is restricted to the long-term debt channel so it does not duplicate the equity-issuance signals elsewhere in the batch. Conditioning concentrates the bet inside the high-cash-yield group, where the value-trap versus true-discount distinction is economically live, while expensive firms receive scores near zero and stay out of both legs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Buyback Surprise Among Cheap Firms
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 1), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The information content of a buyback is in the change, not the level: mature firms repurchase every year and that steady-state flow is already in prices and in the investment factor, whereas a cheap firm that sharply steps up net repurchase activity relative to last year is delivering new evidence that management sees the discount as unwarranted.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the payout level with a first difference strips the persistent component that loads on CMA and leaves a news-like variable, which is the most direct repair of the alpha-absorption failure diagnosed above. Scaling the flow by assets rather than market value keeps the change from being mechanically driven by the price move already embedded in the valuation moderator, so the two legs of the interaction stay economically independent.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Industry Relative Cheap Self Funded Payout
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Enterprise multiples are set at the industry level, so a firm cheap relative to its own industry peers while returning capital funded internally rather than by new borrowing is mispriced, whereas the raw cross-sectional EV multiple mostly ranks industries and therefore reproduces a static value tilt.
considered.reasoning: This isolates one specific design choice against the best generation-0 result (fmb 3.90, alpha +0.010): swapping the cross-sectional rank for an industry rank in the valuation moderator, holding the internally-funded capital-return leg fixed. If the industry-neutral version raises the FF5 alpha while keeping the slope, it confirms that the missing alpha was an industry/value-tilt artifact rather than a defect of the payout-funding mechanism.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap Firm Buyback Over Dividend Tilt
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, dvt), at), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Payout composition, not payout size, encodes valuation opinion: dividends are a smoothed commitment insensitive to price, while repurchases are discretionary and price-contingent, so a cheap firm tilting its payout mix toward buybacks and away from dividends is expressing a view that its own shares are the best available investment.
considered.reasoning: Total payout yield is a known, factor-spanned characteristic, but the buyback-versus-dividend mix is roughly payout-neutral and therefore should not inherit the HML/CMA loadings that flattened the generation-0 alphas. Conditioning the mix on cheapness gives the interaction its economic bite, since a buyback tilt at a rich valuation carries the opposite information about managerial judgment.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Net Cash Valuation Repurchase
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: When a large fraction of market capitalization is covered by net cash on the balance sheet, the operating business is being valued at almost nothing; management repurchasing shares in that state is converting excess liquidity into the cheapest asset it can buy, while a firm in the same state issuing equity signals that the cash is committed or the business is impaired.
considered.reasoning: Net cash to price is a valuation metric that HML (book-to-market) spans poorly because book equity mixes cash with operating assets, so the value tilt that absorbed prior alphas should be much weaker here. The interaction is economically necessary: high net cash alone is a known low-return "cash trap" characteristic, and it only becomes bullish when management demonstrably deploys the cash into its own undervalued equity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap Equity For Debt Swap
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(MIN(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: When managers believe their equity is cheap relative to their debt, the value-maximizing action is a capital-structure swap — raise long-term debt and retire shares — so a cheap firm doing both simultaneously is making a costly, leverage-increasing bet on its own stock, while a cheap firm doing the reverse swap (selling equity to repay debt) is deleveraging under duress and confirms the discount is warranted.
considered.reasoning: The financing leg is no longer a net payout yield, so this is not a rescaling of book-equity-retired-per-market-dollar: the MIN operator requires both debt issuance and equity retirement to be positive, isolating genuine recapitalizations from ordinary cash-funded buybacks and from debt raised to fund capex. Direction is now internally coherent — the non-negative cheapness rank means overvalued issuers sit near zero rather than in the long leg — and the signal deliberately contrasts with the accepted self-funded-payout proposal, so the batch tells us whether the funding source of a buyback helps or hurts.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Unlevered Cheap Repurchaser
considered.expression: MUL(MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness means mispricing only when the firm has the balance-sheet slack to act on it: a low-leverage firm trading at a high book-to-market that retires equity is buying a discount it can afford, whereas an equally cheap but heavily indebted firm is priced for leverage risk and its financing choices are dictated by creditors rather than by managerial valuation opinion.
considered.reasoning: This drops all past-return and valuation-change conditioning, so it is not a horizon variant of the contrarian-buyback signal; the new conditioning axis is the leverage state, a financing-theme variable that separates distressed value from mispriced value. Because the MIN conjunction damps highly levered deep-value names — exactly the firms whose returns FF5's HML and CMA loadings already explain — the surviving spread should be less factor-spanned and more likely to show abnormal return rather than a repackaged value tilt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Industry Neutral Both Legs Capital Return
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Payout and issuance norms are as industry-specific as valuation multiples — utilities and banks systematically pay out, biotech and tech systematically issue — so the informative part of a firm's capital-return decision is its deviation from peer practice, and pairing that deviation with industry-relative cheapness should isolate firm-specific managerial conviction.
considered.reasoning: Industry-ranking only the valuation leg already lifted alpha from 0.010 to 0.014 and Sharpe from 0.35 to 0.42, so the natural next question is whether the residual factor exposure sits in the financing leg's industry composition. IND_ADJ demeans the capital-return intensity within industry while preserving its sign and magnitude, which keeps the economic content intact and removes the sector bets that likely load on CMA and RMW.

considered.name: Cash Conversion Enterprise Yield Capital Return
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: EBITDA overstates distributable cash for firms with heavy working-capital absorption or non-cash revenue, so measuring enterprise cheapness with realized operating cash flow should identify firms whose capital return is genuinely fundable and screen out accrual-inflated cheap multiples.

considered.name: Dividend Commitment Increase At Cheap Enterprise Value
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(dvt, 1), at), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Dividends are a sticky commitment that management is reluctant to reverse, so raising the dividend is a costlier and more credible statement about future cash flow than a discretionary buyback; a cheap enterprise increasing its dividend is signalling durable earnings power, while a cheap enterprise cutting it is confirming impairment.

Using the asset-scaled first difference rather than dividend growth keeps non-payers in the sample at zero, preserving coverage while letting initiations and cuts drive the tails.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Sustained Claim Contraction At Cheap Enterprise Value

considered.hypothesis: A revenue-based enterprise multiple identifies firms whose operating scale is cheaply priced without conditioning on current margins, so it captures temporarily depressed but structurally sound businesses that an EBITDA multiple classifies as expensive; combined with credible earnings and capital return, this should locate mispricing that profitability-linked value measures miss.

considered.name: Accrual Inflated Issuance At Rich Enterprise Value
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1)))

Enterprise-value scaling and an industry-ranked richness weight avoid the negative-book-equity misclassification and the RMW-spanned profitability tilt that undermined the earlier short-side attempts.

considered.name: Cash Certified Claim Contraction
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), SUB(ib, oancf)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Credibility belongs inside the financing measure, not beside it: the economically meaningful quantity is the capital a cheap firm returns in excess of the paper earnings it booked without collecting, so subtracting the accrual gap from the capital-return flow yields a single measure of claim contraction that is actually financed by realized cash.
considered.reasoning: This diagnoses the slope dilution directly rather than by permuting rank combinators: the archive's fmb fell from 3.78 to 2.36 precisely when a third noisy rank was stacked multiplicatively, and folding the accrual gap into the flow restores the two-term structure that produced the strong cross-sectional evidence while retaining the credibility content that produced the alpha. Both the payout and the accrual correction are now measured in the same units and scaled by the same enterprise value, so the construction is a genuine netting rather than a weighting.

considered.name: Own History Payout Position When Cheap

considered.reasoning: Centering the within-firm rank fixes the sign inversion the critic identified — the own-history position now enters symmetrically, so firms at their historical financing extremes populate the two tails in the intended order instead of the magnitude of the current flow determining the ordering. The signal is now purely ordinal in the time dimension and nonnegatively weighted by cheapness, which also removes the outlier sensitivity of the raw EV-scaled flow that governs the incumbent's extreme deciles.

considered.name: Unusual Payout With Credible Earnings
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at))), MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5))))

considered.reasoning: These are the archive's two largest alphas (0.030 and 0.023) and they operate on different objects (the timing of the decision versus the quality of its funding), so the combination tests whether their contributions are additive or a single effect measured twice. The cost is coverage falling to roughly 0.078 and the known risk of triple-product dilution, which is exactly why the batch retains full-coverage single-channel versions as controls.

considered.reasoning: The cross-sectional cheapness rank is precisely the component that loads on HML and has repeatedly been absorbed by FF5, so replacing it with a within-firm valuation position should push the whole interaction into the factor-orthogonal space where the generation-6 alpha was found. This is the logical completion of that discovery rather than a repeat of the earlier contrarian-buyback signal, which paired a within-firm book-to-market rank with a cross-sectional payout *level* and therefore never tested the within-firm financing dimension.

considered.name: Cardinal Payout Deviation From Own Norm

considered.hypothesis: The economically relevant quantity may be how far this year's capital return departs from the firm's own normal level, in real magnitude rather than in rank order — a firm that ordinarily returns one percent of assets and this year returns eight is making a much larger statement than one that moves from the fortieth to the eightieth percentile of a narrow personal range.
considered.reasoning: This isolates a single, economically substantive design choice against the generation-6 winner: ordinal within-firm position versus cardinal within-firm deviation, holding the valuation leg and the flow definition fixed. If the cardinal version fails, the alpha is attributable to the robustness of ordinal measurement against lumpy annual financing flows, which would be a genuine finding about how this class of signal should be built.

considered.name: Unusual External Capital Raising At Rich Value
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)))), ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: The overvaluation half of the story should obey the same within-firm logic: a richly valued firm raising equity and debt at the top of its own five-year fundraising range is exploiting a window it does not normally have, whereas a firm whose capital raising is at its habitual level is simply running its standard financing policy and carries no timing information.
considered.reasoning: Every previous short-side attempt used a cross-sectional issuance level, which FF5 already prices through CMA and RMW and which delivered wrong-signed alphas; the within-firm fundraising position is the one formulation that has not been tried and is the mirror of the design that just produced the archive's best alpha. considered.name: Improving Capital Return Trajectory When Cheap

considered.hypothesis: A firm whose capital return has been rising steadily for five years while its shares stay cheap is on a path of increasing shareholder orientation — a management transition, an activist outcome, or a business turning cash-generative — and that trajectory is more informative about the future than any single year's position within the range.
considered.reasoning: Position within a range and slope through it are distinct temporal concepts: a firm can sit at its five-year high after one lumpy year with no trend, or trend strongly upward without hitting an extreme, so this is not a horizon variant of the generation-6 winner but a different statement about the financing process. It also tests directly whether the market underreacts to gradual policy change, which the failed multi-year cumulative sum could not detect because it summed levels rather than measuring direction.

considered.name: Payout Unusual Beyond The Earnings Cycle
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Most of the variation in a firm's capital return is mechanical — companies distribute more in their good years and retrench in bad ones — so the discretionary, information-bearing component is the part of the payout's within-firm position that exceeds the within-firm position of its own profitability: a cheap firm returning capital at its five-year high while its margins are only mid-range is making a deliberate statement, not riding a cyclical peak.
considered.reasoning: This is not an average of the two financing legs already tested — it is a *difference* between two within-firm ordinal positions, which purges the earnings cycle from the financing signal and leaves only the managerial discretion the mispricing story actually relies on. The construction is naturally signed and centered without any winsorization, so the short leg is populated by cheap firms whose payout lags their own earnings position (retrenching despite a good year), which is a different and more diagnostic short leg than any prior design produced.

considered.name: Two Sided Payout Trajectory

considered.name: Shareholder Payout Trajectory When Cheap

considered.reasoning: This is a component test of the winning signal with a clear economic prediction: if the shareholder-only trajectory matches or beats alpha 0.038, the mechanism is managerial payout policy, and if it deteriorates, the mechanism is genuinely about total claim contraction including deleveraging. considered.name: Steady Deleveraging At Cheap Value
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), NEG(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at), 5), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The trajectory that matters for a cheap firm may be on the liability side rather than the payout side: a company that has reduced its net debt burden year after year is steadily transferring enterprise value from creditors to shareholders and lowering the risk that forced the discount, whereas a cheap firm whose net debt has been climbing for five years is on a path toward distress regardless of what it currently pays out.

Because it uses only balance-sheet items it needs no cash-flow-statement financing data, giving it a coverage profile and a failure mode independent of the payout-trend family.

considered.reasoning: This replaces the unstable slope-over-volatility ratio with a second trend rather than a division, so there is no small-denominator degeneracy, and it makes both legs dynamic — a divergence-of-trajectories interaction that no archive signal has tested, since every prior version paired a static valuation level with a dynamic financing measure. considered.hypothesis: A cheap firm returning far more capital than its own five-year norm is acting on a discount the market has not recognised, while an expensive firm returning far less than its own norm — that is, newly consuming capital — is funding a premium it cannot sustain internally; each departure from the firm's own policy baseline is informative in the valuation corner where it is economically damning.

considered.expression: ADD(MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), ADD(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1), ABS(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1)))), MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)))), NEG(ADD(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 5), 1), ABS(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 5), 1))))))
considered.hypothesis: The two halves of the story are about different corporate actions, not two signs of one action: undervaluation is revealed by a cheap firm progressively returning more capital, while overvaluation is revealed by an expensive firm progressively going to the capital markets more often, and gross external raising captures that second behaviour far better than the negative tail of a netted payout flow.
considered.reasoning: The current champion uses the same netted variable on both sides, so its short leg is "cheapening payout" rather than "increasing market dependence"; giving each side the financing object its own economics calls for is a substantive change rather than a reweighting. The gross-raising trend previously failed as a standalone signal, but that test paired it with a valuation level and no long leg — here it functions only as the short half of a structure whose long half is independently established.

considered.name: Two Sided Trajectory Against Multiple Path
considered.expression: ADD(MUL(RANK(TREND(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 5)), ADD(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1), ABS(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1)))), MUL(RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 5))), SUB(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1), ABS(WINSOR(TREND(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), at), 5), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Mispricing is a divergence of paths: the strongest long case is a firm whose multiple has been compressing for years while it returns steadily more capital, and the strongest short case is a firm whose multiple has been expanding for years while it returns steadily less, because in both the market and management have been moving in opposite directions for long enough that one of them must be wrong.
considered.reasoning: The one-sided version of this dynamic-versus-dynamic idea scored alpha 0.029 with t 3.01, and the two-sided weighting lifted the static-valuation version from 0.038 to 0.043, so combining them tests whether the valuation leg should be a level or a path once the financing leg is a path. It is the only construction in the archive in which both legs are trajectories with each side weighted by the matching direction of re-rating.
